items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.

items.link_text: 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2: Patrick died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (source S3, PA death certificate). Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so a certificate exists; its informant and stated parents' names are the closest direct parent naming. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable. Verify against the image.

The tree cites the 1850 census (Patrick ~5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84; I1 birth ~1845 'Ireland' conflicts with the objective's 'Pennsylvania', so birthplace must be tested) and lists S2, the 1860 census. United States Census, 1860 is name-searchable; check whether Patrick is still with Thomas and who else (a mother, siblings) is in the household.

Free before paid: United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Patrick would be ~25, possibly still in a parental household or newly married; find him and any Flynn household nearby (Thomas, a widowed mother, siblings). 1870 gives birthplace per person but not relationships, so pair with other items.

Requested by the researcher. 1870 United States Federal Census (Ancestry, paid index, Pennsylvania). A second index with different transcription can surface Flynn spelling variants (Flinn, Flin, Flyn) missed on FamilySearch. Search Patrick Flynn b. ~1845 in Schuylkill and neighboring counties; log 1850 Ancestry search was positive, so capture handoff applies.

Flynn is likely Roman Catholic; loc_001 says registers stay with the Philadelphia diocese/parish, not the county. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable: look for Patrick's baptism (~1845), siblings' baptisms naming Thomas and a mother, and Patrick's own marriage and burial entries. Try variants Flinn, Flin.

Subject's own burial entry and cemetery record. A baptism may not exist (birth place unresolved, Ireland vs Pennsylvania, and parish registers may start late or sit in Ireland), so burial/cemetery entries giving age, birthplace or kin are the fallback route. Look in the parish where he last lived, March 1908.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (~b. 1818) to Patrick's mother: Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (name-searchable), plus Catholic marriage registers. It would confirm the couple as a unit, give a mother's name (possibly a prior married name, so not treated as maiden name), and date the union relative to Patrick's birth. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Marriage may have occurred in Ireland.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could die anywhere from 1850 to ~1890s or later, so window is set by his lifespan, not Patrick's. Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse Schuylkill Register of Wills images for a will or administration naming Patrick as heir. Also check a mother's estate.

FAN item: neighbors of dwelling 84 in 1850 and Patrick's possible siblings. Siblings' death certificates, marriages and baptisms often name the same parents; neighbors in the 1850 and 1860 pages may be kin or fellow immigrants from the same Irish parish, bearing on Patrick's origin.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree holds Thomas Flynn only as b. ~1818 Ireland with no death fact and no sources; proof summary ps_001 lists his probate as unsearched. loc_001: Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811, naming heirs. Window set by Thomas's plausible lifespan (alive 1860, died up to ~1905), not Patrick's. FAN value: heirs, executors, bondsmen, appraisers and witnesses are kin or neighbours who can link Patrick to Thomas. Check FamilySearch PA probate coverage first; browse if personCount 0.

Re-read the 1850 (dwelling 84) and 1860 (dwelling 112) pages for neighbours: households on adjacent lines with Flynn or Irish-born families of similar ages, and any Flynn in the same household who could be a mother or sibling. Neighbours are potential kin and chain-migration companions; the earlier searches only recorded Patrick and Thomas. Neither census states relationships.

1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses are unsearched (ps_001). 1880 states relationship to head: look for Thomas Flynn with Patrick as son, or elderly Thomas or a widow living with Patrick, and for siblings of Patrick in adjacent households. Also trace son-in-law James Brown's household for in-laws.

Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland, so a baptism in Schuylkill parish registers may not exist (and the 1850 census puts the family in PA when he was 5). Plan Patrick's own marriage (1865-1885) and his burial entry (March 1908; death certificate gives death 1908-03-12), which commonly state age, origin and parents. Catholic registers are held at the parish or Archdiocese of Philadelphia (loc_001), not the county; also look for sponsors at the baptisms of Patrick's children, who are often siblings or cousins. Death-certificate informant James Brown is a son-in-law, so identify the daughter's marriage too.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother (likely before 1845, possibly in Ireland, which needs its own locality survey) and for Patrick's possible siblings' baptisms and marriages in the coal region naming Thomas. Confirms the couple as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name, but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child; pair with sibling records placing the family together. Treat any surname for the mother as possibly a prior married name.

Obituary for Patrick Flynn (d. 12 Mar 1908) and any obituary for Thomas Flynn: obituaries name surviving siblings, pallbearers and relatives from other towns, which are FAN names pointing to the family group. Reveals the associates to pursue in other items.

Burial location of Patrick Flynn and cemetery plots adjoining: Thomas Flynn and probable wife or siblings may share the plot or lie in neighbouring lots, and burial records name lot-holders. Gives independent evidence of family grouping where census gives none.

Naturalization of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland) and of Irish neighbours; declarations list witnesses who vouched for residence, often kin. Loc_001 notes coal-region naturalization films can be browse-only, so browse images if not name-searchable. Also land deeds for Thomas Flynn, where adjoining owners and witnesses are FAN names and a later deed from Thomas to Patrick would link them.

- pli_007, census, Schuylkill, 1850-1860, FamilySearch. Re-read the neighbors on the 1850 and 1860 pages for kin and chain-migration companions.

Patrick Flynn's parents are still not proved. The census and his death certificate point to Thomas Flynn, but none of them says "father and son" in a way that settles it. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

sources.citation: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Recorder of Deeds, Deed Book 42, p. 118, Patrick Sheahan from James Kelly, 1875; FamilySearch digital images.

entry.rationale: Tree records Michael with a 1870 residence only in 'Pennsylvania' and a 1882 Schuylkill residence as Miner (no source attached to either). The name-searchable 1880 census shows where he lived and worked just before the move (a mining district elsewhere would support a work-driven move, a farm or non-mining job would cut against it) and whether he lived with relatives. Search Sheahan with variants Shehan, Sheehan, Shean, Sheehan.

Tree gives only 'Pennsylvania' for 1870 with no source. The name-searchable 1870 census establishes his earlier household, age, birthplace and occupation, anchoring identity before the 1880 and later census and showing whether he was already a miner.

FAN item. Brother Patrick Sheahan purchased land from James Kelly in 1875 (Deed Book 42 p. 118, S1), seven years before Michael's recorded 1882 residence, so a family-pull reason is a rival to the mining tradition. Check that deed's content, grantor/witness names, and any later deeds or transactions involving Michael or Patrick. Per loc_001 laborers often leased from mining companies, so absence of Michael deeds is expected.

The Schuylkill County church records collection is name-searchable. Per loc_001 Catholic registers sit with the parish, Archdiocese of Philadelphia. Look for Michael, Patrick and their children's baptisms, marriages and burials: sponsors, residence and stated origin parish test the family-pull versus mining-work explanations, and show which mining town they settled in.

Name-searchable 1900 and 1910 censuses (the 1890 census was largely destroyed, so no substitute exists there). They show Michael's occupation, years in the US, birthplace, naturalization status, and neighbors/boarders from the same origin, testing whether he stayed in mining. Window runs past 1882 because later records testify to the earlier move.

Name-searchable Pennsylvania county marriages (from 1885) and death certificates (from 1906; statewide registration began 1906 per loc_001) for Michael's own marriage and death. They state age, birthplace, parents, occupation (e.g. miner, or cause of death such as miners' asthma) and residence duration, so they may give his origin and prior home.

Naturalization records (loc_001 says coal-region naturalization images are partly browse-only: browse image-by-image) may give arrival date, prior residence and witnesses who were co-workers or kin. Use only if census shows him foreign-born. Use volume_search for Schuylkill volumes when executing.

Pennsylvania probate is browse-only (personCount 0): browse Schuylkill Register of Wills for estates of Michael, Patrick, or their parent (the Sheahan parent I3 is unnamed). Window is set by the lifespans of Michael and Patrick, not the 1882 move. Wills and estates name heirs and sometimes origin; employer-related debts or accident claims may show mining work.

Local coal-region newspapers (e.g. via Chronicling America or newspapers sites) and mine-accident reports, employer or Pennsylvania mine inspectors' annual reports may name Michael as employee, injured miner or newcomer, and record colliery openings or strikes around 1882 that would explain labor recruitment. Contextual evidence for the mining-work hypothesis.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Tree facts (S1, unverified compiled data): Michael resided in Pennsylvania in 1870 (place unspecified) and in Schuylkill County as a Miner in 1882. The 1870 and 1880 United States censuses are name-searchable. They test where he was before 1882, whether he already worked as a miner or laborer, who he lived with (possibly Patrick), and birthplace. The 1880 schedule records relationship to head of household. Search spelling variants Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan, Shean.

The 1880 census predates the move and the 1890 census is largely lost, so the 1900 and 1910 censuses (name-searchable) show whether Michael stayed in Schuylkill County, his occupation (miner, laborer, other), his immigration or birth state, and year of immigration. Sized beyond the 1882 window because they testify to the work he did after the move.

FAN item. Tree source S2 records Patrick Sheahan (I2, brother, same parent I3) buying land from James Kelly in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42, p. 118), seven years before Michael's 1882 move. This suggests chain migration through family. Re-read the deed image for the residence, occupation and witnesses, and search the Recorder of Deeds index for Michael and Patrick 1875-1890 (loc_001: coal-region land was often leased, so a laborer may have no deed). James Kelly and witnesses are associates who may reveal the Sheahan connection to the county.

Name-searchable Schuylkill County Church Records. Baptisms of Michael's children, his marriage, sponsors and burial entries often state a home parish or origin and name family or neighbors. loc_001: Catholic registers sit under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia and are held at the parish, so a parish-by-parish check may be needed. Pre-1906 events have no civil vital records. Also search Patrick's events as a FAN check on the family's arrival date.

Michael's own death certificate (name-searchable from 1906) and county marriage records (name-searchable from 1885) give occupation, birthplace, parents' names and years of residence. Death was likely after 1906. Death entries may state cause (e.g. miner's asthma) and usual occupation, which bear on the mining question. Civil marriages begin after the move, so also use item 4 for earlier marriages.

Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill County wills and estates for Michael, Patrick and the parent I3. Window is set by the creators' lifespans, extending decades past 1882. Estates name heirs and relatives and may mention the family's origin or prior residence.

Local coal-region newspapers (e.g. via Chronicling America or newspapers.com, to be located) may report mine accidents, strikes, hirings, arrivals, and obituaries naming Michael or Patrick. Obituaries often state when and why a man came to the region. Also covers industry context: 1870s-1880s labour conditions and colliery openings that would support or contradict the coal-work motive.

Employer and occupational records: colliery and coal company payrolls, mine inspectors' annual reports (which list accidents and fatalities), and county histories or miners' benevolent society records. These directly test whether Michael worked in a mine and for whom, which census occupation alone cannot show. Locate holding repositories (e.g. county historical society, state archives) before requesting.

Naturalization records, if Michael was an immigrant, may be in browse-only coal-region image groups (loc_001). They state prior residence and arrival date, helping separate a move from elsewhere in Pennsylvania from an earlier immigration. Check with a volume_search before browsing. Whether he immigrated is unverified; the 1900 census item should settle it first.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Patrick Flynn age 15 in household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. Consistent with 1850 placement.
Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

entry.rationale: The 1860 census (log_004) already shows Patrick Flynn age 15 in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County, so pl_002 covered 1860; this item continues the trail. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Patrick would be about 25, probably married or boarding, so search Patrick Flynn b. ~1845 with variants Flinn, Flin, Flynne, and also search Thomas Flynn b. ~1818 in the county, since Thomas may head a separate household. Note the tree records Patrick's birthplace as Ireland while the question says Pennsylvania; read the stated birthplace on each entry and record it. Record neighbours (FAN) as possible kin. 1870 does not state relationships, so co-residence is only suggestive.

United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and is the first schedule to state relationship to head and each person's parents' birthplaces, so it is the best census for testing Thomas as Patrick's father if Thomas, age ~62, lives in Patrick's household or nearby. Search both men with spelling variants; check birthplaces of parents against the Ireland/Pennsylvania discrepancy. Schuylkill County has been stable since 1811 (loc_001), so no boundary issue; check adjoining townships and neighbouring households as FAN evidence.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and states relationship, birth month and year, and parents' birthplaces, and it is the last census before Patrick's 1908 death. Thomas would be ~82, so a look for him in Patrick's household, or in a daughter's, would be direct evidence; the 1908 death certificate informant was son-in-law James Brown (log_005), so also check for Patrick in or near that family. The 1890 census was destroyed, so 1900 is the only schedule in that gap; note that the 1890 schedule does not exist rather than planning it.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, cited to S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates), but the tree holds no parents' names from it. The state certificate (1906 onward, per loc_001) normally names father, mother and informant. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable. The mother's name here may be a married name; treat it as a lead. Verify against the image.

The tree already holds the 1850 census (S1: Patrick, birth ~1845 Ireland; Thomas Flynn ~1818 Ireland is his recorded father via R1) and 1860 (S2). The 1850 schedule gives no relationships, so Thomas as father rests on co-residence alone (Standard 11). The 1880 census records relationship to head and parents' birthplaces, so it is the key later year; add 1870 and 1900 to track Patrick's household and any elderly parent living with him. The existing census collection is listed under externalCollections for Schuylkill. Note the tree says Ireland while the question says Pennsylvania; the 1880 birthplace entries help settle it.

Baptism of Patrick and siblings, if born in Schuylkill. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Per loc_001, Catholic registers sit with the parish and the Philadelphia diocese, not the county. If he was born in Ireland (tree fact F1) a baptism here will not exist, and no parish register start date is known, so items 4 to 6 work back from the end of his life. Search variants Flynn, Flinn, Flin, O'Flynn and Patt/Patrick.

Patrick's own burial entry and cemetery record after his 1908-03-12 death. Because a baptism may not exist (Irish birth in tree, parish unknown), the burial register, obituary and cemetery record may state age, birthplace or parents. Uses the name-searchable church collection; follow up with parish and cemetery sexton records and local newspaper obituary.

Patrick's own marriage (about 1865-1880 for a man born ~1845). Marriage entries may state birthplace and parents' names. County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable; before 1885 use church marriage registers. Also gives his wife's name for later FAN work.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (~1818) to Patrick's mother, kept separate from baptism searches. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (maiden name only if it was her first marriage; do not assume), and by date relative to ~1845 corroborate Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. If they married in Ireland this will fail, which is itself informative about the origin. Sources: church records and Civil Marriages, both name-searchable. Search the Flynn name variants.

Estate of Thomas Flynn at the Register of Wills (held from 1811 per loc_001). Window is set by the father's lifespan: born ~1818, he may have died any time up to about 1900 or later, so the window is not capped at Patrick's life. A will or administration naming Patrick as heir is direct parentage evidence. Pennsylvania, Probate Records is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets. Also check Patrick's own 1908 estate for sibling heirs.

FAN item. Other Flynn households in the 1850 and 1860 census neighbouring Thomas, plus Patrick's likely siblings: their baptisms, marriages and death certificates, and sponsors or witnesses at Patrick's marriage. These could name the same parents, which a father-only census co-residence cannot show. Use name-searchable church and death collections; make a brother or sister's 1906-1908 death certificate a priority.

Naturalization papers for Thomas Flynn (and Patrick, if he came as a child). Per loc_001, coal-region naturalization films are often browse-only image groups, so check with volume_search and browse image by image. Declarations may give Irish origin, arrival date and port, pointing to where to look for the family abroad.

After those it browses probate files for his father Thomas, looks at neighbours and siblings, and finishes with naturalization papers that might show where the family came from in Ireland.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain — 1835-1870

Before civil registration (1871) the parish books are the vital record. Santa María's books from 1837 are on FamilySearch, unindexed but full-text searchable; one births volume for 1841-1845 is name-indexed.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: Tree holds only a birth of about 1843 at Vélez-Málaga for I1, no parents and no sources. Civil registration began 1871 (loc_001), so the baptism is the primary record and normally names both parents and the four grandparents. The 1841-1845 births volume is 96% name-indexed: search María Josefa García Romero with variants (Josepha, Josefa, Garcia/Garzía, Romero). Also try the name-searchable Spain, Baptisms collection and Catholic Church Records. Naming customs page: the double surname is normally father's then mother's, but treat that as unconfirmed until the entry names the parents.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: Fallback if the index misses (about 'about 1843' leaves a window, and indexing may miss variants). The Santa María books from 1837 are browse-only for name search (record-indexed 0%) but full-text searchable. Run a full-text search on García and Romero as co-occurring separate terms, unscoped, with the search-full-text approach, not a phrase search of the compound name; clerks may swap the surnames, so which is the father's stays unsettled. Covers image groups 004104131 for 1837-1895 and 1842-1848.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, once a candidate couple appears. It confirms them as a couple, supplies the mother's surname (only her first marriage gives her maiden name; check for remarriage) and by its date relative to c.1843 corroborates parentage, though it does not alone prove María Josefa is their child. Search Spain, Marriages (name-searchable) and Santa María marriage books. Window set by the parents' likely marriage before the birth, 1815 to 1843.

FAN item: baptisms of siblings and of her own children, and godparents named in her baptism. Siblings' baptisms name the same parents and test whether the García Romero couple is consistent; godparents are often kin. Window is set by the parents' child-bearing years. Use Spain, Baptisms (name-searchable) and Santa María books.

Subject's own marriage entry (marriage and pre-marriage records commonly state age, parents' names and origin) and her own death/burial entry. Her marriage date is unknown; search Spain, Marriages and Spain, Deaths (both name-searchable) and Santa María marriage and death books. These are the usual route if the baptism entry cannot be found, since the birth is only 'about' 1843.

Civil death record and Málaga Municipal Records (name-searchable) for her death, and civil registers after 1871, which name parents and age. Window runs to 1930 because her death could fall well after 1871.

Contingency: foundling and orphanage records for Vélez-Málaga are browse-only (full-text searchable). If no baptism naming parents is found, test whether she was an abandoned or orphaned child. Fallback to the baptism search.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Pennsylvania County Marriages: Martin Kearney m. Bridget (Doyle) Halloran, 1879, Schuylkill County. Confirms Bridget's second marriage and that her first married surname was Doyle, maiden name Halloran. Found incidentally while researching an unrelated question; not part of any plan.

query.description: 1900 census page image, Schuylkill County, PA - Kearney household, fertility columns

items.notes: Original 1900 census image for the Kearney household: 'Mother of how many children' = 9; 'Number of these children living' = 2. Indicates Bridget bore ~9 children, most likely during the earlier Doyle marriage, with only 2 surviving to 1900. Only one of the two, Ellen Doyle, has been identified by name so far. Roughly 7-8 children remain unidentified/undocumented.

Pennsylvania County Marriages: entry for Ellen Doyle's own marriage, with her parents recorded as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Independently identifies the first husband's given name as JOHN Doyle. Found incidentally; not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree survey: Bridget Halloran born ~1838 Ireland (no source); John Doyle has no facts; Ellen Doyle's tree entry has no dates. log_003 shows Ellen's marriage (1865-1875 search window) naming John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Households of John and Bridget Doyle in the 1860, 1870 and 1880 censuses (name-searchable) list the children living at home; 1880 also gives relationship to head. loc_001 says Schuylkill is coal-region, so also try neighboring county spellings Doyle/Doyl/Doil. Bridget remarried Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001), so the 1880 household may list Doyle children as stepchildren.

Pennsylvania civil birth registration began only in 1906 (loc_001), so baptisms are the primary birth evidence. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; search baptisms with father John Doyle and mother Bridget (Halloran) across the Catholic parishes, which sit under the Diocese of Philadelphia per loc_001. Sponsors are FAN leads. Nine births across a ~1855-1878 childbearing span for a woman born ~1838.

Dedicated item for John Doyle and Bridget Halloran's marriage to each other (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages and Compiled Marriages are name-searchable; also church marriage registers). It confirms the couple as a unit, gives Bridget's maiden name Halloran from a first marriage record, and its date relative to the children's births tests the ~9-children count. Marriage may instead have occurred in Ireland or another county; it does not by itself prove any child.

Seven of nine children died before 1900 (log_002), likely in childhood, so baptism may be undocumented and burials are the usual trace. Search church burial entries and cemetery records for Doyle children and for John Doyle's own death; entries often name parents and age. Name-searchable church collection first, then cemetery transcriptions and Find a Grave.

Marriage records of Ellen Doyle and of other Doyle children naming parents John Doyle and Bridget Halloran (Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950, both name-searchable). Per log_003 Ellen's own marriage record already names the parents; re-read its witnesses and bondsmen as FAN leads, and search Doyle marriages with those parents' names to find the 1-2 surviving siblings. Window runs to 1925 as the surviving child's marriage could be later.

Estate files for John Doyle (death date unknown; he predeceased the 1879 Kearney marriage per log_001 where Bridget is a widow) and later for Bridget Kearney. Pennsylvania, Probate Records is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills dockets, held from 1811 (loc_001), not a name search. Heirs named in administrations or guardianships of minor Doyle children are direct parentage evidence. Window sized to John's lifespan to Bridget's likely death.

The 1900 Kearney household (log_002) gave 9 born, 2 living; the 1910 census gives the same fertility columns for Bridget if alive and lets us find the second surviving child among nearby households. Name-searchable. Also search neighbors and adult Doyle children living near Ellen as FAN.

Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 (name-searchable) for Bridget Kearney, Martin Kearney and Ellen: informants and named relatives point to surviving children; Bridget's certificate names her parents and may give the informant child.

Obituaries and death notices for John Doyle and for Bridget Kearney in Schuylkill County papers often list surviving and predeceased children. Outside FamilySearch; coal-region papers on newspaper sites, executed through external-site search.

items.guide_markdown:
## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Mikkel's birth (20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn); no parents, sources or ark. His baptism entry names both parents and sponsors. Denmark Church Books is name-searchable overall, but loc_001 says Stagstrup is only ~3% name-indexed, so browse the 1779 register images by date (late Aug-Sep 1779). Check variants Mikkel/Michel/Mikkell, Nielsen/Nielsøn, Blyeberg/Bly(e)berg/Blyberg; per the naming-customs page a farm name is residence, not surname, so also expect entry as Mikkel Nielsen alone. Father's given name should be Niels.

Denmark, Military Levying Rolls is name-searchable and, per loc_001 and the military records page, lists boys from birth under the father's name from 1788/89, so Mikkel's entry is direct parentage evidence for a male subject. Search Mikkel b. ~1779 in Stagstrup; place fields may rank rather than filter, so if the index underdelivers, browse the Thisted Amt rolls by parish. Also gives father's name/farm for later death search.

Dedicated search for a marriage of a Niels and a woman, parents of Mikkel, in Stagstrup or neighbouring parishes. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (not assumed to be a maiden name if remarriage appears) and, by date before Aug 1779, corroborate the father. It does not alone prove Mikkel is their child; the baptism or levy roll must place him with them. Window set by a plausible marriage age for parents of a 1779 birth. Browse Stagstrup marriage registers since index is ~3%.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 is name-searchable. The 1787 census (Mikkel age ~8) and 1801 census may show him in a household headed by a Niels, and list neighbours (FAN) who may later appear as sponsors or witnesses. Household co-residence supports but does not alone establish parentage.

FAN/sibling item: baptisms of siblings (children of the same Niels) and the sponsors named in Mikkel's and siblings' entries reveal the family unit, the mother and likely relatives. Naming-pattern custom (first son named for the father's father) helps test candidate grandfathers. Browse register images, since Stagstrup is ~3% name-indexed.

Mikkel's own marriage and death/burial entries, which may name or imply his father (marriage entries sometimes give parentage; burial gives age to confirm the 1779 birth and the parish). Included in case the 1779 baptism is hard to locate or unlegible. Search Mikkel Nielsen with Blyeberg variants across Thisted Amt church books (name-searchable collection; Stagstrup itself browse).

Objective also asks when the father died. Once Niels is identified, search his burial in Stagstrup church books; window runs from Mikkel's birth to about 60 years later, set by the father's lifespan not Mikkel's. Browse images given ~3% indexing.

Denmark Probate Indexes 1674-1851 is name-searchable; an estate (skifte) for the father Niels, or for the mother, would name heirs including Mikkel and give death date. Window set by the father's plausible death between 1779 and 1851 (index end).

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

Tree holds only Birth 1814 Kentucky and Residence 1870 Muhlenberg County, no death fact. loc_001 says statewide death certificates begin 1911, so none can exist for a death in the 1870s-1880s; the premise is tested by a name search of Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (name-searchable) for an Elijah Wilkins born c. 1814 (he would be 97+, so a hit is unlikely and must be identity-checked by birth year and county). Variants: Wilkins, Wilkerson, Wilkens.

County death registers in Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (name-searchable) cover 1852-1910 per loc_001, though 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. A register entry would give death date, place, age and parents, the pre-1911 substitute for a certificate. Search Wilkins variants, then Muhlenberg County with no name filter.

loc_001 names probate as the primary death evidence for this era and says Muhlenberg probate survives well for the 1870s. Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of will books, administrator bonds and estate settlements for Elijah Wilkins. Window runs from the 1870 residence through the 1880s as the death window; extends to 1895 for late settlements.

The 1870 residence is the last-known-alive date; the 1880 census (relationship to head recorded) shows whether Elijah is still alive or a widow or son heads the household, bracketing death to 1870-1880. Plan a national collection lookup for the 1880 census before searching; no 1880 collection is confirmed this session.

Church burial registers and cemetery records (e.g. Find a Grave, county cemetery surveys) can bracket death and give place of burial per loc_001; headstones often carry exact dates. Doubles as a FAN item: adjacent Wilkins family stones may name the widow and adult children who would be administrators.
Local newspaper obituaries or death notices, and notices by an administrator or executor calling on creditors, fix death date and place where registers and probate are silent.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.

entry.rationale: The tree records Patrick's death as 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates). Statewide registration began in 1906 (loc_001), so this certificate exists and Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable. It should name his parents and an informant, and state birthplace; it is derivative evidence only for parentage, so treat names as leads. Read the image, not just the index.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Catholic registers stayed with the Diocese of Philadelphia (loc_001) and are held at parish level. The tree gives birth as Ireland while the objective says Pennsylvania, so a baptism may not exist in any register reachable here; search Patrick's baptism if in PA, and his burial entry (1908, age and birthplace) as the subject's own death/burial item. Try variants Flynn, Flinn, Flin, Lynn, Fflynn.

Patrick's own marriage: because the birth place is contradictory (Ireland in the tree, Pennsylvania in the objective) and baptism may not exist, marriage entries often state age, birthplace and parents. Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and County Marriages 1885-1950 are name-searchable; also marriage entries in the church records. Window covers his likely marriage age from about 20 to 55.

The tree cites the 1850 census (S1: Patrick, about 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, per log_001) and the 1860 census (S2) for the Thomas-Patrick link. The 1850 schedule gives no relationships, so that link is co-residence only (Standard 11). The 1880 census records relationship to head and parents' birthplaces, so prioritise 1880 plus 1870 to see Thomas's household, wife and siblings, and Patrick's own household.

Dedicated parents' marriage item: marriage of Thomas Flynn (tree: born about 1818, Ireland) to a wife not yet identified, about 1835-1850, in civil registers (Civil Marriages and Compiled Marriages, both name-searchable) and church marriage registers. It confirms the couple as a unit and may give the wife's name, but a surname found here may be a prior married name, so do not call it her maiden name; pair with the sibling and probate items. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child.

Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) could die from the 1850s into the 1880s or later, and his wife later still, so the window follows the parents' lifespans, not Patrick's. Register of Wills from 1811 (loc_001); Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill dockets image by image. A will or administration naming heirs is direct parentage evidence. Also check Patrick's own 1908 estate for named siblings or mother.

FAN item: Patrick's possible siblings' baptisms and marriages, and godparents or sponsors and witnesses, in the Schuylkill church records naming Thomas Flynn and a wife as parents; also the neighbours of dwelling 84 in the 1850 census. These reveal the wife's name and the family unit around Patrick, and sponsors often are kin.

Obituary in local Schuylkill newspapers and cemetery or burial records for Patrick around 12 March 1908: obituaries often name surviving siblings and a birthplace, and the cemetery plot may place him beside Thomas or a mother. Leads to verify, not proof.

If Patrick or Thomas was Irish-born (the tree says Ireland), naturalization papers may give an origin county and arrival date. loc_001 notes coal-region naturalization films are browse-only, so browse by image. Also plan a full-text co-occurrence search on Flynn plus the first names of Thomas and the wife, unscoped, if indexed search stalls, to find an Irish-origin baptism.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZKR-BR1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

Tree records Bridget's birth as 1871 in Pottsville with no source and no baptism; parents Thomas Kerrigan (b. 1842 Pottsville, d. 1898 Pottsville) and Ellen Burke (b. 1846 Ireland) are Irish-Catholic names. Pennsylvania civil birth registration began only in 1906 (loc_001), so the baptism register is the primary record. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable: search Kerrigan and variants (Kerrigon, Kerigan, Kerrican, Carrigan), Bridget/Brigid/Bridgit/Biddy, with parents Thomas and Ellen/Helen Burke/Bourke/Burk. Catholic baptisms were often entered in Latin (Brigida, Kerrigan). Baptism usually falls days to weeks after birth, so the window runs to 1873 in case the birth year is approximate. Registers stay with the Diocese of Philadelphia parishes (loc_001), so a Philadelphia-diocese Pottsville parish is the target.

Fallback if the name search fails: the Schuylkill church image group (volume 007936751) is browse-only (personCount 0, 0% record-searchable), so browse image by image for Pottsville Catholic baptism entries in 1871-1872. loc_001 notes coal-region church films are browse-only. The volume also carries German-language content, so confirm the parish is the family's before reading.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Kerrigan and Ellen Burke (Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 are name-searchable; the county marriages collection starts 1885, too late). The marriage places the couple in a parish and may name a church where the baptism would be recorded; it confirms the couple as a unit but does not by itself show Bridget was baptized there. Ellen was born in Ireland c. 1846, so she may have married elsewhere or earlier; check the church collection for the marriage entry too.

FAN item: baptisms of Bridget's siblings to Thomas Kerrigan and Ellen Burke, and sponsors (godparents) named in them. Siblings' baptisms identify the family's parish and the register volume, and sponsors named in Bridget's entry may recur across them, helping separate her entry from other Kerrigan families in Pottsville. Uses the name-searchable church collection.

Thomas Kerrigan died 1898 in Pottsville per the tree (unsourced). His burial or funeral entry in the church collection names his parish, pointing to the family's church for the baptism search; an estate file would be a further lead but Pennsylvania Probate Records are browse-only (personCount 0). Date window is set by Thomas's lifespan.

Bridget's own marriage and death records. Her marriage (name-searchable county marriages collection from 1885, and church marriage entries) and her death certificate (name-searchable death certificates from 1906) may state her age, birthplace or parents, and a church marriage entry often cites the baptismal parish. Gives a cross-check on the baptism date if found, or a route to the parish if it is not. Browse-only marriage volume 007936753 (1870-1910) is a backup.

Question q_001: "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

What the project tree already holds:
- Patrick Flynn (I1) has Thomas Flynn (I2) as his only recorded parent.
- Thomas is also recorded as the father of Mary Flynn (I3) and James Flynn (I4).
- No mother is recorded for any of them.
- Patrick died by 1908.

Active plan pl_002, in order:
- pli_004 (census, Schuylkill County, 1860, FamilySearch): completed. It confirms Patrick in Thomas's household.
- pli_005 (vital record, Schuylkill County, 1908, FamilySearch): completed. It looked for a death certificate naming the parents.
- pli_006 (probate, Schuylkill County, 1870-1890, FamilySearch): in progress, and it is the next step. A will or estate file for Thomas Flynn could name Patrick as a son. The FamilySearch "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" collection is browse-only (personCount 0). That means paging through the county's probate images, not a name search.

Gaps I would raise once pli_006 closes, if the question stays open:
- The plan has no item for the parents' marriage to each other, which would supply the mother's name.
- It has no item for Patrick's baptism or church records. The Schuylkill County church collection is name-searchable.
- It has no FAN items (relatives, neighbours, associates).
- It has no 1850 census or Patrick's own marriage record.
- The question's status and its conclusion are out of step: the question reads as concluded while its stored status is still in progress. That is for the conclusion step to sort out.
- The project has no locality survey for Schuylkill County, which a new plan would need first.

Hand-back: search-records should finish the probate browse (pli_006), then log it.

---

This plan is meant to work out who Patrick Flynn's parents were. So far the searches have placed Patrick as a child in Thomas Flynn's household in the 1860 census and looked for his 1908 death certificate. The step in progress is browsing Schuylkill County probate records from 1870 to 1890 for a will or estate file of Thomas Flynn that names Patrick as a son. Those records have no name index, so they have to be paged through image by image. After that, the plan would still need the parents' marriage, church baptism records and records of relatives and neighbours.

Next, the probate images for Thomas Flynn will be browsed and the result logged, and then the remaining gaps can be planned.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

**Mode:** create (no earlier plans). Question q_001: "In which Pennsylvania county was Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) born?"

**Already in the tree**
- Thomas Hale's birth is recorded as about 1810 in "Pennsylvania", with no county.
- His death is recorded as 1868 in Greene County, Ohio.
- His wife Sarah has no facts.
- Five children, Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, were born about 1836 to 1847 in Greene County, Ohio.
- No sources are attached to anything.
- Thomas has no FamilySearch ark, so there is no hints-review item.

**Plan pl_001**
- **pli_001:** Vital records (death certificates), Greene County, Ohio, 1908–1950, FamilySearch. Children who lived past 1908 may have certificates naming the father's birthplace.
- **pli_002:** Census, Greene County, Ohio, 1840–1870, FamilySearch. Identifies the household, name variants, and neighbors born in Pennsylvania.
- **pli_003:** Marriage of Thomas and Sarah, Greene County, Ohio, 1830–1840, FamilySearch. Bondsmen and witnesses may be kin from Pennsylvania.
- **pli_004:** Probate, Greene County, Ohio, 1868–1880, FamilySearch. A will or guardianship may name heirs and a Pennsylvania residence.
- **pli_005:** Land records, Greene County, Ohio, 1830–1868, FamilySearch. Deeds show prior residence and adjoining owners.
- **pli_006:** Newspaper obituary and county-history sketches, Xenia, Ohio, 1868–1869, other repository.
- **pli_007:** Cemetery and burial records, Greene County, Ohio, 1868–1870, other repository. Thomas's own death and burial entry.
- **pli_008:** Pennsylvania census, 1810–1830, FamilySearch. Candidate Hale households — to run last, once the Ohio items give better identifiers.

No item is a fallback for another. Eight searches in total.

**Notes**
- Catalog lookups returned nothing confirming collection availability; that is noted in pli_001.
- No Pennsylvania locality survey exists yet. Before pli_008 can be narrowed to a county, a locality survey should be run.
- Because no baptism is likely to exist for an 1810 birth in an unknown county, the plan leans on his death, marriage, and children's records.

**Next:** search-records for the FamilySearch items (pli_001–pli_005, pli_008), and search-external-sites for pli_006 and pli_007, beginning with the children's death certificates.
